Attack · InterceptINFO 310 · Jan 2026

Man-in-the-Middle Attack & Credential Interception

Built an isolated attack lab on a Microsoft Azure cloud VM, modeling a full network in GNS3 with separate attacker and victim machines. I ran an ARP spoofing attack to sit between the victim and the gateway, captured traffic in Wireshark, and because the app ran over HTTP, read the victim's login credentials in clear text.

ResultCaptured plaintext credentials off the wire and mapped the impact to the CIA triad, showing exactly why unencrypted traffic breaks confidentiality.
GNS3AzureDockerARP spoofingWiresharkHTTP
▸ Read the write-up
Overview

The purpose of this lab is to understand how a man in the middle attack works and why sending data over an unencrypted network can be risky. This exercise focused on showing how an attacker can intercept network traffic when devices trust the local network and encryption is not used. The goal of the lab was to observe how sensitive information can be exposed during a man in the middle attack.

Instead of using real devices like a phone and a laptop, this lab was done using a virtual setup that my TA provided. I used a cloud virtual machine through Microsoft Azure and ran the entire network inside GNS3. In this setup, I created separate virtual machines that acted as the attacker and the victim, all connected through a switch and a NAT device. This made it possible to simulate a real man in the middle attack in a safe way without putting any real users or networks at risk.

To complete the lab, I used my laptop to access the Azure virtual machine and GNS3 to build the network. I also used a web browser and Docker to run a vulnerable web application, along with an ARP spoofing tool to redirect the victim’s traffic through the attacker. Finally, I used Wireshark to capture and look at the victim’s network traffic. The goal of using this setup was to better understand how man in the middle attacks actually work and why using encryption is important for keeping user data private.

Steps I took

I logged into the Azure virtual machine provided by the TA and opened GNS3. I loaded the lab project that contained a NAT node, a network switch, an attacker machine, and a victim machine, all connected on the same virtual network.

I started all devices in the GNS3 and confirmed that the attacker and victim machines were both connected to the switch and had network access through the NAT node.

On the attacker machine, ran the ARP spoofing command in the terminal, targeting the victim machine. This caused the attacker to position itself in the middle of the network traffic between the victim and the network.

After the ARP spoofing attack was successfully running, I opened Wireshark on the attacker machine and began capturing packets on the network interface connected to the switch.

On the victim machine, I opened a web browser and navigated to the vulnerable web application running through Docker.

I logged into the web application from the victim machine using the provided credentials while Wireshark was actively capturing traffic on the attacker machine.

Once the login process was complete, I stopped the packet capture in Wireshark. I applied filters to view traffic coming from the victim machine and filtered by the HTTP protocol.

By inspecting the captured packets, I was able to view the login request and see the credentials in clear text, confirming that the man in the middle attack was successful.

Figure
Key findings

What is the specific asset you were able to obtain from your MITM?

The specific asset obtained during this man in the middle attack was the victim’s login credentials. Because the victim accessed the web application using HTTP, the username and password were sent across the network in clear text. By placing the attacker machine in the middle of the communication, I was able to capture this information directly from the network traffic using Wireshark.

Which CIA properties were violated in this attack and how were those properties violated?

The primary CIA property violated in this attack was confidentiality. Confidentiality was broken because sensitive information, such as login credentials, was transmitted without encryption and could be read by an unauthorized party. The victim assumed that their data was private, but the lack of encryption allowed the attacker to view the information directly. Integrity and availability were not directly affected, since the data was not changed and the service remained accessible.

Which specific values did you spoof?

During this attack, ARP values were spoofed. The attacker machine sent false ARP messages to both the victim and the network gateway, claiming to be the other party. This caused both systems to associate the attacker’s MAC address with trusted IP addresses. As a result, the victim’s traffic was redirected through the attacker machine without the victim knowing.

Takeaway

What stood out the most was how simple the attack actually was. Seeing login credentials show up in clear text made it clear that serious security issues do not always come from advanced or complex attacks. In this case, the problem came from basic choices like using HTTP instead of HTTPS and relying on network protocols that trust any response they receive. This lab helped me understand how attackers often take advantage of normal system behavior rather than breaking things outright.

The lessons from this lab can be used in other situations by being more aware of what systems assume is safe. Going forward, I can apply this way of thinking when looking at networks or applications by asking where trust exists and how it could be misused. This mindset is useful not only for finding weaknesses, but also for building stronger defenses. Overall, this lab made it clear why encryption and secure network design are so important for protecting user data.

Defense · EncryptINFO 310 · Jan 2026

Securing Web Traffic with TLS / HTTPS

Closed the exact weakness the MITM lab exposed. I generated a key and CSR with OpenSSL, signed the certificate with the iSchool root CA, and configured nginx through Docker to serve the app over HTTPS on port 443 — then re-ran the capture to prove the traffic was now protected.

ResultVerified end-to-end encryption in Wireshark and explained which OSI layers stay in clear text after TLS, and why.
OpenSSLnginxTLS / SSLPKIDockerWireshark
▸ Read the write-up
Overview

This lab focuses on understanding how cryptography protects data when it is sent over a network. We saw that unencrypted web traffic can be intercepted through the lab, man in the middle attacks, allowing sensitive information to be exposed. The goal of this exercise is to secure a web application by enabling HTTPS and then verify that the data is encrypted during transmission. To complete this exercise, tools such as OpenSSL are used to generate security certificates, Docker and nginx are used to host the application securely, and Wireshark is used to observe network traffic. Together, these tools help demonstrate how encryption prevents attackers from reading sensitive data, even when traffic is intercepted.

Steps I took

Open terminal and navigate to certs folder where certificates will be stored.

Use OpenSSL to generate a private key and a certificate signing request (CSR). This command creates a public and private key pair for the local website and saves them as localhost.key and localhost.csr.

At this point, the certificate request needs to be approved so the website can prove its identity. Since this project runs locally, the provided iSchool Root CA is used to sign the request. This process creates a certificate named localhost.crt, which allows the web application to use HTTPS and encrypt data sent to and from localhost.

Open docker-compose.yaml file to use HTTPS. Update the file to tell them where our certificate and private key are located. Update the exposed port so the router listens on port 443 instead of port 80.

Edit the nginx configuration file to listen on port 443 with SSL enabled. Add the paths to the certificate and private key so nginx knows where to find them inside the container.

Redeploy the Docker containers in terminal. Once running, open a browser and navigate to https://localhost:443. Proceed past the browser warning to confirm the site loads over HTTPS.

Open Wireshark to confirm that the connection was encrypted and set it to capture loopback traffic on the local machine. While it is running, access through https://localhost:443.

Make sure the captured traffic is using TLS which indicates that encryption was active.

Figures
Key findings

Q: What layers of the OSI model remain in clear text following our encryption implementation?

A: After HTTPS is enabled, only the lower network layers remain in clear text. The Physical layer and Data Link layer still send raw signals and frames so data can move across the network. The Network layer (IP) and Transport layer (TCP) also remain visible because devices need this information to route packets and keep connections working. However, everything above these layers, including HTTP data at the Application layer, is encrypted by TLS, which prevents anyone from reading the actual content of the communication.

Q: Which CIA Properties are protected that were previously violated during the MITM attack?

A: The main CIA property that is now protected is confidentiality. During the MITM attack, sensitive data such as login information could be read in plain text. After encryption is applied, this data is no longer readable, even if traffic is intercepted. Integrity is also improved because encryption helps detect if data is changed during transit. Availability was not the main issue in the attack, since the service was still accessible before and after encryption.

Q: Why is encryption alone insufficient for establishing a fully trusted connection?

A: Encryption alone is not enough because it does not prove who you are communicating with. Even though data is encrypted, an attacker could still create their own certificate and pretend to be a trusted website. This is why trusted Certificate Authorities (CAs) are important. A trusted CA verifies the identity of a website and allows the browser to confirm that the connection is real. Without a trusted CA, the connection is encrypted but not fully trusted.

Takeaway

From this lab, it became clear that encryption is a powerful tool for protecting confidentiality, but it is not perfect on its own. Even though the data was encrypted, the browser still warned that the certificate was not trusted. This shows that encryption alone does not guarantee trust. A trusted Certificate Authority is also needed to verify identity and prevent attackers from pretending to be a legitimate website. If someone wanted to break or bypass the cryptography used in this lab, they could try to trick users into accepting a fake or untrusted certificate or perform social engineering to get users to ignore browser warnings. An attacker could also target weak certificate management or outdated encryption settings. This shows that security depends not only on strong cryptography, but also on proper configuration and user awareness.

Overall, this lab showed how cryptography protects data during transmission and how attackers think when trying to intercept or bypass security. It also demonstrated that real security requires both technical controls and trust, not just encryption alone.

Monitor · DetectINFO 310 · Feb 2026

Security Logging & Brute-Force Detection

Instrumented a PHP password-manager app with centralized logging using Monolog and Loggly, recording failed and successful logins, logouts, and unauthorized access. I then added brute-force protection that counts failed attempts per IP, triggers a lockout, and logs the detection event.

ResultBuilt detection-and-response logic (per-IP lockout plus alerting) on top of full security-event logging, so misuse is both recorded and stopped.
LogglyMonologPHPMySQLDockerBrute-force defense
▸ Read the write-up
Overview

This lab focuses on understanding how logging is used in cybersecurity to track activity and detect possible attacks in a web application. The goal of this exercise is to set up logging for a PHP-based password manager and use those logs to record important security events such as failed login attempts and other user actions. By adding logging, we can see what is happening inside the system and identify behaviors that could be unsafe or suspicious. This lab uses Loggly as the logging service, along with Docker, PHP, MySQL, and the Monolog library to send and view logs. Through this exercise, I learned how logging supports security monitoring and helps protect applications from misuse.

Steps I took

Create a Loggly account and copy the customer token from the Loggly dashboard. Add this token to the .env file as LOGGLY_TOKEN, then pass it into the PHP container using the docker-compose.yaml file.

Start the application using Docker and open the password manager in the browser. Open Loggly in a separate tab and set the log time window to “Last Hour” so new logs are visible.

Add the loggly-logger.php component to the components folder and include it in login.php, logout.php, and other required PHP files. Confirm the test message appears in Loggly to verify logging is working.

On the login page, enter an incorrect username or password and submit the form. The page shows an error message, and a failed login event appears in Loggly. Repeat this step to confirm each failed login is logged.

Enter the correct username and password and submit the login form. The application verifies the credentials, sets the authentication cookie, and redirects the user to the main page. At the same time, a successful login event is sent to Loggly using an informational log that includes the username, confirming that successful login attempts are being tracked.

Log out of the application using the logout button. When logout is triggered, the application reads the authenticated username from the cookie and sends an informational log to Loggly recording that the user logged out. The authentication and administrator cookies are then cleared, and the user is redirected back to the login page.

After logging out, manually type the URL of a protected page into the browser. Because there is no authentication cookie, the application blocks access, logs an unauthorized access event to Loggly, and redirects back to the login page.

Next, log in again with valid credentials and access the same protected page. This time, the page loads successfully, and an authorized access event is logged in Loggly with the username and page information.

Adding brute-force protection

In login.php, add brute force protection logic by defining a maximum number of failed attempts and a lockout time.

Modify the login request logic so that each time the form is submitted, the script first checks whether the client IP is currently locked out. If the lockout is active, display a warning message and log a brute force block event to Loggly.

Update the failed login logic so that every incorrect username or password increments the failed attempt counter for the client IP and logs a failed login warning to Loggly.

Add logic to detect when the failed attempt count reaches the maximum allowed value. When this happens, set a lockout timer and log a brute force detection event to Loggly that includes the IP address, username, number of failed attempts, and lockout duration.

Update the successful login logic so that when valid credentials are entered, a successful login message is logged to Loggly and all brute force counters for the client IP are reset.

Start the application using Docker and open the login page in the browser. Open Loggly in another tab and set the log time window to “Last Hour.”

Submit the login form with incorrect credentials multiple times. Each failed attempt generates a warning log in Loggly and increases the failed attempt count.

After the fifth failed attempt, submit the form again to trigger the brute force detection. The application blocks further attempts, displays a lockout message, and logs both brute force detection and block events.

Figures
Key findings

Q: The goal of cybersecurity is to protect assets. There are three ways we have discussed protecting assets. In terms of the methods we have discussed, how does logging help protect assets?

A: Logging helps protect assets because it’s basically like leaving a trail of receipts for what happens in the app. It shows what someone tried to do, when they did it, and which user (or sometimes which IP) was involved. So if someone keeps failing logins over and over or tries to open a page they shouldn’t be able to see, the logs make that obvious instead of it happening quietly. And if something bad does happen, logs let you go back and retrace what happened step-by-step, instead of guessing.

Q: Where did you add logging? Why did you choose that location to add logging?

A: In login.php, I logged failed logins, successful logins, and the brute force stuff. I picked this file because this is the first place someone tries to get into the app. If anything, sketchy is going to happen, it usually starts here, so it made sense to track it right at the login step. In logout.php, I logged when a user logs out (with their username). I chose this because it helps show when someone’s session ends. It’s also just good for tracking normal account activity, like “this person logged out at this time.” In authenticate.php, I logged both unauthorized and authorized access. I chose this because this file is what protects the locked pages. So if someone tries to jump straight to a protected page without logging in, it logs that attempt. And if someone is logged in and gets in normally, it logs that too. It’s a simple way to prove the access control is actually working.

Q: As we continue to enhance and secure the UW Password Manager application, what other user actions do you believe should be logged?

A: As we keep improving the UW Password Manager, I think we should log more of the “important” actions that deal with sensitive stuff or big changes. For example, it would be useful to log when someone creates a new password entry, edits one, or deletes one, because those actions change what is stored in the vault. Another action worth logging is when someone copies a password, because even though it seems normal, it can help explain what happened if something looks off later. On top of that, logging account setting changes (like changing a user password) and any admin-only actions (like creating users, deleting users, or changing roles) would make the system easier to audit and harder to abuse without being noticed.

Takeaway

In this lab, I learned that logging is kind of like having a security camera inside your app. The app can still “work” without logs, but you have no real way to know what people are doing or what went wrong until it’s too late. Once I set up Loggly, it clicked for me that logs aren’t just for debugging, they’re how you catch patterns. Like, if someone keeps failing login over and over, or they try to open a page they shouldn’t be able to see, logging is what turns that into something you can notice and prove instead of just guessing.

Logging works with the hacker mindset, but it also makes you think like the attacker. On the defense side, logging helps you spot weird behavior faster. It also gives you a timeline so you can go back and see what happened step by step. But if I think like a hacker for a second, I’m also asking, “How do I avoid being seen?” In this lab, we blocked after 5 failed tries from one IP, so a hacker could try to spread attempts out across different IPs, use a VPN, or just slow down their attempts so it doesn’t look like a fast brute force. Logging makes it harder for attackers to hide, but it also pushes them to be more careful and sneakier. If someone wanted to spoof or get around the logging we made, there are a few ways. Since the brute force tracking is stored in the session, they might try to reset their session or clear cookies to try to get a fresh start. Since the lock is based on IP, they could also switch networks or use a VPN to get a new IP and avoid the lockout. Another thing is that if someone puts strange input into fields like the username (like extra symbols or long text), they might try to make the logs messy or harder to read. And in the worst case, if someone ever got access to the server itself, they could try to mess with the logging setup completely, like stopping logs from being sent or hiding what they’re doing.

The main lesson I’m taking from this lab is that logging should be part of security from the start. If an app has logins, roles, or sensitive data, then it should log the key moments: failed logins, successful logins, logouts, access blocked/allowed, and big actions like creating, editing, or deleting important data. At the same time, this lab also showed me that logging isn’t magic. It helps you see what happened, but you still need strong protection in the app itself. For me, logging is like leaving footprints, if the footprints are there, you can catch problems faster, and if something goes wrong, you can actually explain what happened instead of just saying, “I think someone hacked it.”

Data · AnalyzeGEOG 461 · Feb 2026

Spatial Risk Analysis: Emergency Incident Density Mapping

Turned thousands of Kent Fire Department call records into clear risk patterns using kernel density estimation and contour mapping in ArcGIS Pro. I standardized projection, cell size, and search radius across five incident types so each map could be compared fairly.

ResultConverted raw NFIRS-coded point data into decision-ready maps with a repeatable geoprocessing workflow.
ArcGIS ProKernel Density (KDE)Spatial analysisNFIRS dataCartography
▸ Read the write-up
Overview

Fire and emergency medical teams need to know where calls happen most often so they can plan staffing, station coverage, and equipment placement. In this project I mapped five types of incidents across the Kent Fire Department service area, turning thousands of individual call locations into clear patterns that show where demand is highest and lowest.

Method

I built the density surfaces with Kernel Density (KDE) in ArcGIS Pro, standardizing the analysis so every map could be compared fairly: the same projection, a 50-foot output cell size, a one-mile (5,280-foot) search radius, and square-mile area units across all five incident groups. I then generated contour lines with explicit, hand-chosen break values tuned to each incident type, and applied consistent symbology so the five layouts read the same way.

Figures
What the maps show

All Responses and EMS are the most widespread and track population and road networks. Structure Fires and Fire/Haz Mat are more limited and cluster in built-up areas, while Service Calls fall in between with several moderate clusters. Using different contour values per incident type keeps rare events (structure fires) and high-volume events (EMS) both readable without exaggerating or hiding patterns.

Takeaway

Kernel density combined with contour intervals is an effective way to turn many individual calls into clear, comparable patterns that support staffing and station-placement decisions — insight that would be hard to see from raw points alone.
